newsitem.title: UK: British central bank urges interest rate rise.
newsitem.headline: British central bank urges interest rate rise.

text.p: The governor of Britain's central bank said on Monday it would be dangerous for the government to delay a rise in interest rates just because a strong pound was helping to dampen inflation.

In an unusually forthright speech prepared for delivery to bankers in Edinburgh, Eddie George renewed his call for a "modest pre-emptive" increase in interest rates to prevent a resurgence in inflation.

The normally circumspect central bank chief said strong growth in money supply and consumer spending could not be sustained for long without jeopardising the government's 2.5 percent for underlying inflation.
Rapid falls in unemployment and the recovery in the housing market were further signs that demand might be strengthening.
"That, essentially, is why the Bank has been arguing that we will need at some early stage a modest pre-emptive tightening of monetary policy," George said.
"We need to anticipate what is to come and begin to moderate the pace of the upswing before the evidence of imbalance comes through into the statistics."
The call poses a dilemma for the ruling Conservative Party, which has been trying to keep rates down ahead of a general election that must be held no later than May 22.

Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke left official interest rates unchanged at six percent at his last regular monthly meeting with George on January 15, citing sterling's strength as a key factor in his decision.
A strong pound helps to reduce inflation by making it cheaper for British companies to buy imported goods.
George's comments suggested that he had advised an interest rate rise at that meeting and was over-ruled and would probably resume his case at the next meeting set for February 5.

In an implicit rebuttal of Clarke's arguments, George said a a persistently strong pound would have only a one-off dampening effect on perhaps a quarter of the goods covered by the retail price index, the main measure of inflation.
When a similar dilemma was faced in the 1980s, the domestic expansion was allowed for some time to continue unchecked.
"But in the end we were driven to bring it to a jarring halt," George said.
"I do not suggest for a moment that we are anywhere close to that situation now. Our aim is precisely to avoid that.

"But that experience does illustrate that, in the final analysis, there could be real dangers in allowing justified concern about the exchange rate to deflect us for too long from moving gradually to moderate the upswing."
George said the dilemma also served to illuminate the debate about a planned single European Union currency.
On the one hand, the real attractions of fixed exchange rates, especially to manufacturers, were amply apparent.

"On the other hand, our dilemma -- and we are not alone in this dilemma within Europe -- points up the problem that would arise if the single European monetary policy -- the single interest rate -- does not meet the domestic monetary policy needs of all the euro-member countries," George said.

The central bank chief said he hoped European political leaders appreciated the crucial importance of sustainable convergence to the success of monetary union and did not just see it as a technical obstacle to their wider aspirations.
"I should like to think that," he added, stressing the word "like.'
